title: CIBN Banking
issuer: Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public CIBN syllabus (banking operations, financial systems, banking law, management). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A customer pays a cheque drawn on another bank into her account and asks when the funds will become available. Through which arrangement are cheques exchanged and settled between the two banks?
options: Through the clearing house operated under the Nigerian Inter-Bank Settlement System
Through the salary payroll platform of the customer's employer
Through the receiving branch's own cash till
Through a private agreement between the two account holders
items.explanation: Cheques drawn on one bank and presented through another are exchanged and settled at the clearing house, which nets the positions of the participating banks. A branch till handles only cash, and payroll or private arrangements do not settle inter-bank obligations.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank customer signs an instruction authorising the bank to pay a fixed amount monthly to a landlord until further notice. What has the customer given the bank?
options: A direct debit allowing the landlord to collect from the account
A standing order to make the regular payments automatically on the agreed dates
A letter of credit opened in favour of the landlord
A bill of exchange drawn by the landlord on the customer
items.explanation: A standing order is a continuing authority from the customer to the bank to pay a fixed sum on specified dates without further instruction. A direct debit is the reverse arrangement, initiated by the beneficiary rather than the payer.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank customer issues a cheque with two parallel lines drawn across its face and nothing written between the lines. What effect do the lines have on the cheque?
options: The cheque becomes invalid and must be returned to the drawer
The cheque may be paid in cash only to the named payee
The cheque must be paid into a bank account and cannot be cashed over the counter
The cheque must be endorsed by two signatories before payment
items.explanation: Two parallel lines across a cheque constitute a general crossing, which requires the cheque to be collected through a bank account rather than paid in cash across the counter. Crossing restricts payment but does not invalidate the cheque.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A company opens a current account and lodges a board resolution naming two signatories who must both sign every cheque. What has the customer established with the bank?
options: A guarantee that the bank will not require any signatures at all
An overdraft facility that the bank must grant on demand
A lien over the company's assets in favour of the bank
A mandate binding the bank to act only on the joint signatures of both signatories
items.explanation: A mandate is the authority the customer gives the bank describing who may operate the account and how. Where it requires two signatures the bank must not honour instructions given by one signatory alone.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: Before opening a new account for a walk-in customer, a bank officer collects a means of identification and proof of address. Which regulatory duty is the officer performing?
options: The customer due diligence required under anti-money laundering rules
The liquidation of the customer's previous bank
The sale of an investment product to the customer
The computation of the customer's income tax
items.explanation: Customer due diligence, commonly called know your customer, requires a bank to identify and verify a customer before establishing a relationship and is a core anti-money laundering control. It is not a sales or tax function.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A customer deposits a cheque payable to himself and writes his signature on the back of it. What is this act called?
options: A crossing of the cheque by the drawer
An endorsement of the cheque by the payee
An acceptance of a bill of exchange
A discounting of the instrument
items.explanation: Writing a signature on the back of a negotiable instrument to transfer it is an endorsement. Crossing is a direction on the face, acceptance relates to bills of exchange, and discounting is a form of lending against the instrument.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank grants a customer a facility that allows the account to go into debit up to an agreed limit for a stated period. What type of facility has been granted?
options: A fixed deposit placed with the bank
A savings account with no withdrawal limit
An overdraft facility repayable on demand
A letter of credit issued for imports
items.explanation: An overdraft permits the current account to be drawn beyond the credit balance up to a limit and is normally repayable on demand. A fixed deposit is a placement by the customer, and a letter of credit is a trade finance instrument.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank holds a customer's title documents as security for a loan while the customer keeps ownership of the underlying asset. What form of security arrangement is this?
options: An outright sale of the asset to the bank
A promissory note issued by the borrower
A bill of exchange accepted by the bank
A lien or charge over the documents rather than a transfer of ownership
items.explanation: Depositing title documents creates a lien or charge that gives the bank rights over the security without transferring ownership. A sale would transfer title, and promissory notes and bills are separate negotiable instruments.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A customer uses an automated teller machine card at a machine belonging to another bank and the transaction succeeds. How is the transaction settled between the two banks?
options: Through an inter-bank switching and settlement arrangement that moves value between the banks
By the customer paying cash to the other bank later
By cancelling the transaction at the customer's branch
By the two banks exchanging physical cash at the end of the month
items.explanation: Card transactions at another bank's machine are routed through a switch and settled between the banks through agreed inter-bank settlement channels. The customer does not separately repay the other bank in cash.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A business customer asks the bank to collect payment from its debtors by obtaining their prior authority to debit their accounts on agreed dates. Which service is the customer requesting?
options: A standing order payable to the debtors
The direct debit collection service
A letter of credit opened in favour of the debtors
A bill for collection discounted by the bank
items.explanation: A direct debit lets a creditor collect payment from a debtor's account after the debtor has authorised the bank to honour the debits. A standing order works in the opposite direction, issued by the payer rather than the beneficiary.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A customer presents a cheque that is more than six months old. How should the bank ordinarily treat such a stale cheque?
options: Pay it immediately because cheques never expire
Pay it only in cash over the counter
Decline to pay it unless it is revalidated or confirmed by the drawer
Return it to the payee for want of a signature
items.explanation: A cheque presented after a long period, commonly six months, is regarded as stale and the bank should seek confirmation from the drawer before paying. A stale cheque is not automatically void, but it is not paid on its face.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank customer wants to keep funds in a foreign currency for a future overseas payment. Which account should the bank recommend?
options: A naira savings account with no foreign exchange features
A fixed deposit held in naira only
A current account held in the name of the bank itself
A domiciliary account denominated in the foreign currency
items.explanation: A domiciliary account is denominated in a foreign currency and allows the customer to hold and remit foreign exchange. Naira accounts do not preserve the foreign currency value of the funds.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank teller receives cash from a customer and must ensure the transaction is properly recorded. Which document does the teller issue as evidence of the deposit?
options: A deposit slip or teller-stamped acknowledgement of the amount received
A share certificate representing ownership in the bank
A promissory note payable to the customer
A mortgage deed over the customer's property
items.explanation: The teller acknowledges a cash deposit on a deposit slip or equivalent stamped record showing the amount and date received. Share certificates, promissory notes and mortgage deeds relate to entirely different transactions.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank discovers a suspicious pattern of large cash deposits that do not match a customer's known business. What is the bank required to do under anti-money laundering rules?
options: Return the deposits quietly to the customer
Report the suspicious transaction to the appropriate authorities promptly
Close the account without keeping any record
Increase the customer's overdraft limit to absorb the cash
items.explanation: A bank must file a suspicious transaction report with the relevant authority when activity is inconsistent with a customer's profile. Quietly ignoring or concealing the pattern would breach anti-money laundering obligations.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A customer keeps valuable jewellery in the bank's strong room under a sealed envelope arrangement. What service is the bank providing?
options: An unsecured personal loan against the jewellery
A guarantee to sell the jewellery on the customer's behalf
A safe custody service for the customer's valuables
An investment in the bank's own shares
items.explanation: Safe custody, sometimes called safe deposit, is a bailment under which the bank stores the customer's valuables and returns them on demand. It is not a loan, a sale mandate or an investment in the bank.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank's electronic banking platform allows customers to transfer funds and pay bills from a mobile phone. Which risk is most directly increased by offering this channel?
options: The risk that the bank runs out of physical cash in its vault
The risk that branch staff forget how to count currency
The risk that customers stop using cheques entirely
The risk of unauthorised access and fraud through compromised credentials
items.explanation: Electronic channels raise the risk that fraudsters obtain a customer's credentials and initiate unauthorised transfers, so authentication and monitoring controls are critical. The other options are not the primary risk created by the channel.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank agent in a rural community collects deposits and opens accounts on behalf of a licensed bank under a written agreement. What model of service delivery does this describe?
options: Agency banking conducted under an approved agreement with the bank
An illegal parallel banking scheme
An insurance brokerage arrangement
A stockbroking service for the capital market
items.explanation: Agency banking allows an approved third party to provide specified banking services, such as deposit taking and account opening, on behalf of a licensed bank under agreed terms. It is a regulated arrangement, not an unlicensed operation.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A bank reconciles its internal ledger of customer balances against the records of the central bank settlement account. Why is this reconciliation performed?
options: To set the interest rate charged on all loans for the year
To confirm that the bank's records agree with the settlement position and to detect errors or fraud
To decide which customers should be offered employment
To determine the exchange rate of the naira
items.explanation: Reconciliation compares two independent records to confirm they agree and to surface discrepancies that may indicate error or fraud. Interest rate setting, employment decisions and exchange rate determination are unrelated functions.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Operations and Practice

items.stem: A company needs short-term funds for ninety days and the bank offers a negotiable instrument issued by the central bank. Which instrument is most likely being described?
options: A preference share issued by a quoted company
A debenture secured by a floating charge
A treasury bill issued by the central bank on behalf of the government
A unit trust investment traded in the capital market
items.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term debt instruments issued by the central bank on behalf of the government and traded in the money market. Preference shares and debentures belong to the capital market and are longer term.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A bank accepts deposits from savers and lends part of those deposits to borrowers who need funds. Which function of the financial system does this illustrate?
options: The direct sale of government policy
The collection of company income tax
The printing of legal tender currency
Financial intermediation between surplus and deficit units
items.explanation: Financial intermediation channels funds from surplus units, the savers, to deficit units, the borrowers, through an institution such as a bank. Printing currency and collecting tax are functions of the central bank and the revenue authority.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A pension fund manager buys newly issued shares directly from the issuing company. In which market does this transaction take place?
options: The primary market where new securities are first issued
The secondary market where existing securities trade
The money market for short-term instruments
The foreign exchange market for currencies
items.explanation: A new issue of securities sold by the issuer to investors occurs in the primary market. Subsequent trading between investors takes place in the secondary market, while the money and foreign exchange markets handle different assets.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A central bank reduces the policy interest rate to encourage borrowing and spending. Which policy stance is the central bank adopting?
options: A contractionary fiscal policy
An expansionary monetary policy
A contractionary monetary policy
An expansionary fiscal policy
items.explanation: Lowering the policy rate is an expansionary monetary action intended to reduce the cost of credit and stimulate demand. Fiscal policy involves government spending and taxation, not central bank rate decisions.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: Inflation rises sharply and the central bank fears it will erode purchasing power. Which action would the central bank most likely take?
options: Reduce the policy rate to encourage more borrowing
Increase government spending on new roads
Raise the policy rate to tighten monetary conditions
Direct banks to lower their lending rates
items.explanation: To curb inflation the central bank tightens policy by raising the rate at which it lends, which raises the cost of credit and dampens demand. Raising government spending would add to demand and worsen inflation.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A country's exports exceed its imports over a year. What does this imply about its trade balance?
options: The country records a trade deficit for the year
The country has a perfectly balanced trade account
The country's currency must become worthless
The country records a trade surplus for the year
items.explanation: When the value of exports exceeds the value of imports the trade balance is in surplus. A deficit is the opposite case where imports exceed exports, and a balanced account means the two are equal.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: An investor compares the return on a government security with the return on a corporate bond of similar maturity. What does the higher yield on the corporate bond represent?
options: A risk premium compensating for the greater possibility of default
A tax imposed only on corporate bonds
A fee paid to the stock exchange
The effect of a fixed exchange rate
items.explanation: The extra yield on a corporate bond over a comparable government security compensates the investor for bearing credit and liquidity risk. It is not a tax, an exchange fee or a currency effect.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A bank holds only a small fraction of its deposits as cash and invests the rest in loans and securities. What principle of banking does this describe?
options: The full reserve system requiring all deposits to be held in cash
The fractional reserve system under which only part of deposits is kept liquid
The barter system of exchanging goods directly
The gold standard linking money to gold coins
items.explanation: Fractional reserve banking keeps only a portion of deposits as liquid reserves and uses the balance to create earning assets. A full reserve system would require all deposits to be held idle as cash.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A central bank requires banks to hold a minimum fraction of their deposits as reserves. What is this requirement intended to influence?
options: The colour of the naira notes in circulation
The number of branches a bank may open
The banks' capacity to create credit and the growth of money supply
The names of the members of the bank's board
items.explanation: The reserve requirement constrains how much of each deposit a bank can lend, so it influences credit creation and the money supply. It has no bearing on the physical notes, branch numbers or board composition.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A newly established company needs long-term equity capital to expand its factory. Which market is most appropriate for raising such funds?
options: The money market where instruments mature within a year
The inter-bank market for overnight lending
The foreign exchange market for currency trading
The capital market where long-term securities are issued
items.explanation: Long-term equity and debt capital is raised in the capital market through instruments such as shares and debentures. The money and inter-bank markets provide short-term funds, and the foreign exchange market trades currencies.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A depositor wants to be sure her savings are protected if her bank fails. Which institution provides deposit insurance to depositors of licensed banks?
options: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Securities and Exchange Commission
The Federal Inland Revenue Service
The Nigeria Customs Service
items.explanation: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation insures deposits held with licensed banks and pays compensation up to a limit on a bank failure. The other bodies regulate securities, collect taxes or administer customs.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: The central bank sells government securities in the open market to commercial banks. What is the intended short-term effect?
options: To inject fresh reserves and loosen conditions
To withdraw liquidity from the banking system and tighten conditions
To raise the prices of shares on the exchange
To reduce the country's import duties
items.explanation: Selling securities takes money out of the banking system as banks pay for them, which drains reserves and tightens liquidity. Buying securities would have the opposite, liquidity-injecting effect.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A financial institution accepts small savings from low-income earners and lends to small businesses in its locality. Which type of institution is most likely described?
options: A primary mortgage institution issuing long-term housing loans
A discount house dealing in treasury bills only
A microfinance bank serving the financially excluded
A bureau de change selling foreign currency
items.explanation: Microfinance banks mobilise small savings and extend credit to micro and small enterprises, particularly those outside formal banking. Mortgage institutions, discount houses and bureaux de change have narrower mandates.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: The government spends more than it collects in revenue during the year. How is this situation described?
options: A fiscal surplus available for distribution
A balanced budget with no financing need
A trade surplus arising from exports
A fiscal deficit requiring borrowing or other financing
items.explanation: When government spending exceeds revenue the budget is in deficit and must be financed by borrowing or other means. A surplus arises when revenue exceeds spending, and the trade balance concerns exports and imports.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Financial Systems and Economics

items.stem: A bank accepts a customer's funds as a deposit and becomes obliged to repay on demand. Which relationship exists between the bank and the customer?
options: A debtor and creditor relationship in which the bank is the debtor
A principal and agent relationship in which the bank is the agent
A landlord and tenant relationship over the customer's funds
A partnership relationship between the bank and the customer
items.explanation: When money is deposited the bank becomes the owner of the funds and owes the customer a debt, so the bank is the debtor and the customer the creditor. Agency may exist for other services, but deposit taking creates a debt.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank reveals a customer's account details to a third party without lawful excuse and the customer suffers loss. Which duty of the banker has been breached?
options: The duty to open a branch in the customer's area
The duty of secrecy owed to the customer
The duty to lend to the customer on demand
The duty to buy the customer's shares
items.explanation: A banker owes a duty of secrecy and must not disclose a customer's affairs except where compelled by law, where the customer consents or where the bank's interest requires. Unlawful disclosure breaches that duty.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A creditor obtains a court order compelling a bank to pay over a judgment debtor's account balance to satisfy a debt. What is this order called?
options: A lien exercised by the bank over its own assets
A charge created by the customer's signature
A garnishee order directing the bank to freeze and pay the balance
A letter of credit issued at the creditor's request
items.explanation: A garnishee order attaches money held by a third party, here the bank, to satisfy a judgment debt, and the nisi stage freezes the balance before the order is made absolute. The other items are different security or payment devices.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank has a general lien over a customer's securities held in the ordinary course of banking. What does a general lien allow the bank to do?
options: Sell the customer's house without any notice at all
Transfer ownership of the securities to the bank permanently
Disregard the customer's written instructions indefinitely
Retain the securities until a debt owed by the customer is settled
items.explanation: A general lien lets the banker retain a customer's goods or securities held in the banking relationship as security for any outstanding balance. It is a right of retention, not an automatic transfer of ownership or a power of sale by itself.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank and its customer owe each other money on the same account and the bank combines the two balances into a net figure. Which right is the bank exercising?
options: The right of set-off between debts owed on the same account
The right to sell the customer's personal property
The right to charge any rate of compound interest
The right to close the customer's private business
items.explanation: Set-off combines mutual debts on the same account so that the net balance is treated as the amount owing. It does not permit the bank to sell other property or to close a business.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank is licensed to carry on banking business in the country. Which statute principally governs the regulation of banks and other financial institutions?
options: The Companies and Allied Matters Act
The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act
The Stamp Duties Act
The Land Use Act
items.explanation: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act regulates the licensing, supervision and operations of banks and related institutions. The Companies Act governs company formation, and the Stamp Duties and Land Use Acts deal with other matters.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank fails and the regulator revokes its licence. Which institution is empowered to insure depositors and manage the liquidation of such a failed bank?
options: The Nigerian Stock Exchange
The National Insurance Commission
The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Bureau of Public Enterprises
items.explanation: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation insures deposits, acts as liquidator of failed insured banks and pays depositors up to the insured limit. The stock exchange, insurance regulator and privatisation bureau have different mandates.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A customer signs a contract of guarantee under which he promises to repay a company's debt if the company defaults. In which capacity is the customer acting?
options: As the principal debtor who is primarily liable
As an agent appointed by the bank
As a trustee holding the bank's assets
As a guarantor who is secondarily liable for the debt
items.explanation: A guarantor is secondarily liable and becomes answerable only if the principal debtor fails to pay. The principal debtor remains primarily liable, and a guarantor is not the bank's agent.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank takes a legal charge over a customer's landed property as security for a loan. What is the practical effect of the charge?
options: It gives the bank a right to enforce the security if the customer defaults
It transfers the property to the bank immediately and permanently
It prevents the customer from ever using the property again
It converts the loan into an equity investment in the customer's business
items.explanation: A legal charge secures the debt and gives the bank an enforceable right against the property if the borrower defaults. Ownership normally remains with the customer, and a charge is not an equity investment.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A customer instructs a bank to stop payment on a cheque that has already been presented and paid. What is the bank's legal position?
options: The bank must reverse the payment and debit the payee instead
The bank already acted on the original instruction and the later countermand is too late
The bank must arrest the payee of the cheque
The bank must pay the cheque a second time to the customer
items.explanation: A stop payment instruction must reach the bank before it acts on the cheque. Once a cheque has been paid in the ordinary course, a later countermand is ineffective and the bank is not liable for the earlier payment.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank employee discloses a customer's account information in order to further a fraudulent scheme. Which offence is most clearly involved?
options: The illegal issuance of legal tender
A foreign exchange allocation error
Fraud and a breach of the duty of confidentiality
A share registration irregularity
items.explanation: Using a customer's confidential account information to perpetrate a fraud is dishonest conduct and a serious breach of the banker's duty of secrecy. It has nothing to do with currency issuance, exchange allocation or share registration.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank wants to appoint a new managing director. Which body's approval is normally required before the appointment takes effect?
options: The local government council of the bank's head office
The customers' forum of the bank
The bank's own external auditors
The central bank acting as the banking regulator
items.explanation: Appointment of senior officers such as a managing director of a bank requires the approval of the central bank, which assesses fitness and propriety. Customers, local councils and auditors do not approve management appointments.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A non-performing loan secured by a mortgage remains unpaid for a long period. Which legal process allows the bank to realise its security?
options: The enforcement of the mortgage through the courts or the applicable recovery process
The immediate deportation of the borrower from the country
The cancellation of the borrower's international passport
The forfeiture of the borrower's salary to the state
items.explanation: A secured lender enforces its mortgage through the courts or the recovery procedure permitted by law to realise the value of the property. Deportation, passport cancellation and salary forfeiture are not debt recovery remedies.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.stem: A bank suspects that funds in an account are the proceeds of crime and continues to operate the account to avoid alerting the customer. What is the bank's proper course under the money laundering regime?
options: Return the funds to the criminals to avoid any trouble
Make the required suspicious transaction report and follow the regulator's guidance on the account
Tell the customer about the investigation immediately
Destroy the account records to protect the customer
items.explanation: A bank must report suspected proceeds of crime through the prescribed suspicious transaction report and follow official guidance, without tipping off the customer. Concealing, returning or destroying records would itself be an offence.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Banking Law and Regulation

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank manager sets objectives for the branch, assigns duties to staff and measures performance against the targets. Which management function is being performed?
options: Auditing the branch's financial statements
Underwriting the branch's insurance policies
Planning, organising and controlling the branch's activities
Printing the branch's currency notes
items.explanation: Setting objectives is planning, assigning duties is organising and measuring performance is controlling, the core management functions. Auditing, underwriting and currency printing are separate activities.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank designs separate savings products for students, salary earners and small traders. Which marketing activity is the bank performing?
options: Market monopoly to exclude all competitors
Currency devaluation aimed at the target groups
Tax planning carried out on behalf of the customers
Market segmentation to serve distinct customer groups
items.explanation: Dividing a market into groups with different needs and serving each appropriately is segmentation. Monopoly, devaluation and tax planning are unrelated to product design for customer groups.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank advertises a new savings account by stressing that it has no maintenance fee and can be opened online. Which elements of the marketing mix are being combined?
options: Product features and promotion communicated to the target customers
Only the price of the bank's own shares
Only the salaries paid to the bank's staff
Only the location of the bank's head office
items.explanation: The advert combines the product, the savings account, with promotion, the message, and touches price through the fee statement. The other options describe unrelated internal matters.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A customer rates a bank highly because staff resolve complaints quickly and keep their promises. Which dimension of service quality is being described?
options: The level of interest paid on customer deposits
The responsiveness and reliability of the service provided
The number of branches the bank operates
The size of the bank's head office building
items.explanation: Prompt complaint resolution reflects responsiveness, and keeping promises reflects reliability, both core dimensions of service quality. Interest rates and branch numbers are not measures of service quality.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank introduces a product and later reviews whether it met its sales targets and customer needs. Which stage of product management is the bank undertaking?
options: The stage of abolishing all products at once
The stage of pricing the bank's shares on the exchange
The evaluation stage that decides whether to grow, modify or withdraw the product
The stage of recruiting a new board of directors
items.explanation: After a product is introduced the bank evaluates its performance against targets to decide whether to grow, modify or withdraw it. This is part of managing the product life cycle, not pricing shares or board recruitment.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank trains its staff to greet customers warmly and handle enquiries politely. Which aspect of service marketing is the bank improving?
options: The bank's compliance with company income tax
The size of the bank's foreign exchange reserves
Only the security of the bank's computer network
The quality of customer service and the overall customer experience
items.explanation: Training frontline staff on courtesy and enquiry handling improves service quality and the overall customer experience. It does not directly affect tax, reserves or network security.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank builds a database of customer transactions and preferences to tailor offers to each customer. Which approach is the bank applying?
options: Customer relationship management using customer data
Currency speculation in the foreign exchange market
Capital budgeting for a new factory building
Auditing the financial accounts of the customers
items.explanation: Customer relationship management uses data about customers to understand and serve them with tailored offers and to build loyalty. Speculation, capital budgeting and auditing are unrelated activities.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank's sales team targets high-income professionals with a premium account that includes advisory services. Which marketing concept does the offer reflect?
options: Selling the same basic product to everyone at the same price
Positioning the product to appeal to a selected target segment
Ignoring the needs of the target customers entirely
Copying a competitor's product without any adaptation
items.explanation: Designing a premium account for a defined segment is positioning, which sets the product apart in the target customers' minds. Offering one undifferentiated product ignores segmentation and positioning.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A branch manager motivates staff by recognising good performance and involving them in decisions. Which management skill is being demonstrated?
options: Auditing that verifies the financial records
Underwriting that assumes insurance risk
Leadership that influences and motivates employees
Clearing that settles inter-bank cheques
items.explanation: Recognising performance and involving staff in decisions are leadership behaviours that influence and motivate people. Auditing, underwriting and clearing are technical banking functions, not leadership.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank compares its strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats before setting a three-year strategy. Which planning tool is the bank using?
options: The cash book of a small trading business
The timetable for clearing inter-bank cheques
The interest rate payable on treasury bills
The SWOT analysis of the bank's internal and external position
items.explanation: SWOT analysis assesses internal strengths and weaknesses together with external opportunities and threats to inform strategy. A cash book, clearing timetable and treasury bill rate serve different purposes.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank wants to reach customers who rarely visit branches by offering services through mobile phones and the internet. Which distribution strategy is the bank adopting?
options: Electronic distribution channels that extend reach beyond physical branches
Closing all of its branches permanently
Withdrawing all of its products from the market
Selling services only to its own employees
items.explanation: Using mobile and internet channels to serve customers is an electronic distribution strategy that extends reach and convenience. It does not require closing all branches or withdrawing products.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank sets the price of a loan product by considering the cost of funds, the risk of default and the rates charged by competitors. Which decision is the bank making?
options: The colour scheme of the bank's new logo
The pricing of the lending product to balance profit and competitiveness
The seating arrangement in the banking hall
The wording of the staff dress code
items.explanation: Pricing a loan involves recovering the cost of funds, allowing for credit risk and remaining competitive. Logo colour, seating and dress code are not pricing decisions.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank measures customer satisfaction and the proportion of customers who remain with the bank over time. Which outcome is the bank monitoring?
options: The bank's liability for company income tax
The number of shareholders on the bank's register
Customer satisfaction and retention as indicators of loyalty
The status of the bank's foreign exchange licence
items.explanation: Satisfaction and retention are the standard measures of customer loyalty and the health of the customer relationship. Tax liability, shareholder numbers and licence status are separate concerns.
items.reference: CIBN Syllabus - Management and Marketing of Financial Services

items.domain: Management and Marketing of Financial Services
items.stem: A bank's marketing department plans the budget for advertising, personal selling and public relations for the coming year. Which activity is the department undertaking?
options: Auditing the bank's annual financial statements
Setting the country's monetary policy
Licensing new banks to operate
Planning the promotion mix to communicate with target customers
items.explanation: Deciding how much to spend on advertising, personal selling and public relations is planning the promotion mix within the marketing function. Auditing, monetary policy and licensing are not marketing tasks.
